subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
passage:
You asked how Gautam and I got married. I'm Jaya, and at twenty-two I came home and told my parents about him. His family belonged to a different community, and my father's face closed like a door. "What will people say? How will they treat you?"

I was furious and nearly packed a bag to say "him or you". My mother stopped me: "First listen to what your father is afraid of." It was fear for me, not hatred of Gautam.

So I gave no ultimatum. For two years Gautam came for Sunday lunch, helped my father mend his radio and never argued. I told them plainly that I would marry him, and that I would never stop visiting them.

At the wedding my father sat stiff at the back. He never said sorry. But he did, once, pass Gautam the last jalebi.

qa.q: What did Gautam help Jaya's father mend?
What was Jaya's father really afraid of?
qa.a: What people would say and how they would treat Jaya. It was fear for Jaya, not hatred of Gautam.

qa.q: What did Jaya do instead of giving an ultimatum?
qa.a: Jaya kept visiting, let Gautam show respect over two years, and said plainly that the marriage would happen while promising never to stop visiting the parents.

qa.q: How might Jaya's father have seen those two years?
qa.a: Probably as slowly showing him that Gautam was steady and kind. Passing him the last jalebi hints at acceptance even without an apology.

grounding: Parents object to Jaya's partner over community; Jaya understands their fear, shows consistency and respect over time, and states what Jaya will not give up.

The power went out in the middle of the argument, and in the candlelight Maria's father's voice sounded even heavier. "A Hindu boy, Maria? What about church, the children, your grandmother?"
Maria's phone buzzed: Ankita, her best friend, texting "did you tell them??" She turned it face down.
She wanted to shout, "Then I'll just leave." Instead she asked, "Papa, what scares you most?"
Silence. Then her mother, quietly: "That you'll lose your faith. That his family won't respect you."
"That's fair to worry about," Maria said. "Siddharth came to Christmas Mass with me last year. His parents have asked to meet you. I'm not asking you to agree tonight. I'm asking you to meet him, once. And I won't give up my faith. I'm sure of that."
Her father stared at the candle. "Once," he said finally.
Later, by torchlight, Maria texted Ankita: "Told them. It's going to be slow. That's okay."

qa.q: What happened in the middle of the argument?
What was Maria tempted to say, and what does it show about her feelings?
qa.a: "Then I'll just leave"; she felt angry and hurt, close to giving an ultimatum.
She asked about her parents' fears, gave concrete signs of respect, asked for just one meeting, and named what she would not give up, her faith.

qa.q: What are Maria's parents afraid of?
qa.a: That she will lose her faith and that Siddharth's family won't respect her.

grounding: Shows parents objecting to a partner of another religion and responding by understanding their fears, asking for time and naming one's own limits instead of an ultimatum.

passage:
Lakshmi's parents in Mylapore had nothing against Akash, they said, except that his father drove an auto and his family was "not our community". For six months they refused to say his name.
Lakshmi didn't give ultimatums. She kept telling them small truths: Akash had cleared his bank exam. Akash had helped her cousin shift flats. And she told them, calmly, the one thing she would not change: "I won't turn someone down just because of their community."
In March her father was admitted to hospital for a knee operation. Akash came every evening after work with coconut water, sat with her mother in the corridor, and left before visiting hours ended, never pushing to be introduced.
On the fourth evening her father, groggy, asked, "Who is that boy who keeps bringing coconut water?" Lakshmi's mother answered before she could. "Akash. He's... polite."
It wasn't approval. But it was his name, said out loud, for the first time.

qa.q: What might Lakshmi have felt when her mother said "Akash" aloud?
qa.a: Relieved and quietly hopeful, since for six months her parents had refused to say his name.

qa.q: What approach did Lakshmi take instead of an ultimatum?
qa.a: She shared small, steady truths about Akash, stated her one limit calmly, and let his quiet respect show over time.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi's mother's view begin to shift?
qa.a: Seeing Akash's quiet care in the hospital corridor, she calls him polite and says his name for the first time.

grounding: Illustrates parents objecting to a partner over community and class, and patient consistency and respect over time instead of burning bridges.
